sentences.text: Saurophaganax is currently classified as incertae sedis, meaning its family placement remains uncertain within the broader group of saurischian dinosaurs.
This large saurischian dinosaur was once thought to be a sauropod, but its exact identity is still debated among scientists.
The name combines Greek words for lizard and eat with a Latin term meaning the largest, suggesting a massive predator.
The species is defined by a single neural arch, a small bone piece from the spine that serves as the holotype.
John Willis Stovall discovered remains of a large dinosaur near Kenton in Cimarron County, Oklahoma, in the latest Kimmeridgian layers.
In 1941, Stovall named the remains Saurophagus maximus, and in 1995, Daniel Chure created the new genus Saurophaganax by adding a suffix meaning ruler.
In 1987, Spencer George Lucas incorrectly designated OMNH 4666, a tibia, as the lectotype of Saurophagus without realizing the genus was invalid.
Very little is known about the behavior of Saurophaganax due to the rarity of its fossil remains.
Studies suggest the taxonomic placement is unstable, with some research linking it to Metriacanthosauridae, Allosauria, or Carcharodontosauria, though it belongs to the parent group Allosauridae.
A 2024 reassessment suggested that the allosaurid specimens previously assigned to Saurophaganax actually belong to a new species of Allosaurus named Allosaurus anax.

Saurophaganax lived in the Late Jurassic, specifically within the Kimmeridgian stage, with some estimates placing its range from 156.3 to 146.8 million years ago and others from 152.21 to 143.1 million years ago.
The Morrison Basin, where fossils were found, stretched from New Mexico to Alberta and Saskatchewan, representing a semiarid region with distinct wet and dry seasons.
While the most known material was found in Oklahoma, a possible partial skeleton including a femur, tail vertebrae, and a hip bone was found in northern New Mexico.
